extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of political history and theory (Florentine history, Machiavellian studies)
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading/exposition of political causes and effects in medieval/early Renaissance Florence (factions, institutions, revolutions) with prescriptive observations about government structure and human nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government must protect both private leaders and the people
rubrics_metrics.description: No nation has a right to blame such a citizen, until they have established a form of government that is capable of protecting him on one side, and the people against him on the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues the fault lies with the constitution rather than the restless disposition of an ambitious individual (example: Corso Donati). If institutions do not provide mutual protection/redress, private ambition and social conflict are to be expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defect in government and wants of the people excite private ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the defect in the government, and the wants of the people, that excite and inspirít the ambition of private men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When government is unable or unwilling to protect citizens from noble oppression, people seek strong leaders (Caffius Maelius, Manlius, Corso) to assist or replace the government; this dynamic explains emergence of popular leaders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppressive constitutions force people to arms and regime change
rubrics_metrics.description: In such a government the people have no protection or security; they are continually oppressed, vexed, and irritated... as the constitution affords no redress, they are obliged to recur to arms and a change of government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If institutional redress is absent, periodic revolt and civil war become the channel for grievances; examples include repeated Florentine uprisings and reliance on foreign princes or dictators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of legislative, executive, and judicial power in one centre is dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: How is it possible, in any simple government, to prevent such management, to draw all the legislative, executive, and judicial power into one centre, and that centre a junto of aristocrats?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage warns against fusing branches of power into an aristocratic junta; it cites governors manipulating imborfations and appointing judges to secure authority as examples of this danger.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation of selection processes increases governors' authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The governors of the city had two ways of maintaining and increasing their authority: one was, by managing the imborfations in such a manner as always to secure the signori either to themselves or their creatures; the other, by getting judges chosen who they knew would be favourable to them in their sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: controlling lotteries/selection and judicial appointments to entrench power (examples: imborfation, creation of favorable judges), which undermines legitimacy and provokes resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substituting lot for regular elections (imborfation) creates long terms that produce mischief
rubrics_metrics.description: They substituted lot in the room of choice... As the lot was not to be now renewed till after a term of above three years, it was thought they had extinguished the causes of all such disgusts and tumults... not being aware how little advantage and how many mischiefs were likely to flow from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although chosen by lot was intended to reduce election-driven faction, long fixed terms and insulation from accountability can produce new pathologies and mischiefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation of military offices can veil absolute power
rubrics_metrics.description: They sometimes constituted a third [judge], whom they called captain of the guards; with which office they now veiled Jacomo d'Agobbio, and gave him an absolute power over the citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing armed offices or commanders under the guise of public safety can be used to concentrate and exercise unchecked authority (example: captain of the guards becoming instrument of oppression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of foreign princes or military leaders relieves external threat but risks internal oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: They applied to Robert, king of Naples, and gave him the government of the city for five years... the duke of Athens... exacted four hundred thousand florins from the city in one year... continually laying some heavy tax or other upon the citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeking external rulers/generals can solve immediate military problems but often substitutes one form of domination for another (heavy taxation, arbitrary exactions, strengthened signori).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government with nobles and commons equally fused leads to noble domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed together, in equal halves, the nobles will for ever tyrannise. The insolence of one side, and the indignation and impatience of the other, at last increased to such a height, that both sides flew to arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation (implicit): separate nobles from commons or structure representation so one class cannot permanently dominate the other; mixing equal halves without safeguards breeds chronic conflict and tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human nature is querulous and discontented; institutions must guard against passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Human nature is querulous and discontented wherever it appears... It is action, not rest, that constitutes our pleasure. All we have to do is to guard and provide against this quality; we cannot eradicate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical institutional design should anticipate and channel human discontent rather than assume contentment; measures should limit destructive effects of restless ambition and factional passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mob rule can be as brutal and tyrannical as monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Human nature is the same in a mob as upon a throne, and that unbridled passions are at least as brutal and diabolical, and unlimited power as tyrannical, in a mob as in a monarch or senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text preserves Machiavelli's graphic description of mob violence (torture, mutilation, cannibalistic imagery) as a warning: replacing tyranny with mob justice risks equally savage outcomes; institutional restraints are necessary post-revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resentment after recovery of liberty can be more severe than resistance to tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater, certainly... is the resentment of the people when they have recovered their liberty, than when they are acting in defence of it; and an instance of brutal ferocity happened here that is a disgrace to human nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautionary principle: periods immediately following liberation often produce excessive vengeance and cruelty; transitional justice should guard against unrestrained popular reprisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disproportionate apportionment of representation empowers elites and causes unrest
rubrics_metrics.description: As the six parts were not duly proportioned, and they designed to give more power and authority to the nobility, it was necessary to make a new regulation in this point, and to increase the number of signori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that how a polity is partitioned for representation (districting/partitions) matters; poorly proportioned divisions can intentionally tilt power toward a class and provoke corrective or revolutionary responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power corrupts across social classes — commons, nobles, and mobs behave similarly when empowered
rubrics_metrics.description: Power has the same effects upon all minds... we find in this instance the Florentine commons discovering the same disposition to tyrannise over all above and all below them, as clearly as ever kings, nobles, or mobs discovered it when they had the power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative supports a general institutionalist caution: any class elevated to unchecked power tends to abuse it; therefore structural checks and balances are required regardless of which class holds authority.
